problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y={e}^{{x}^{3}-4x}$ at the point where $x=2.$
worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={e}^{u},\,u={x}^{3}-4x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}-4.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot (3{x}^{2}-4) \\  & =(3{x}^{2}-4){e}^{{x}^{3}-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=2$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & ={(3{x}^{2}-4){e}^{{x}^{3}-4x}\,|}_{x=2} \\  & =(3(2)^{2}-4){e}^{{2}^{3}-4(2)} \\  & =8\cdot {e}^{0} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$
